items.question: Why prescribe ritual expiation for the unknowing if remembrance alone destroys sin?
premises: The Picu scripture teaches that remembrance alone can destroy sin.
Ritual conduct is still prescribed for the sake of those who do not know the truth.
The Goddess questions how a formal expiation rite is needed if remembrance suffices.
items.inference: The text introduces a tension between the liberating power of remembrance and the continued need for ritual expiation for the unawakened.
uncertainties: The exact identity or scope of the Picu scripture is not specified here.
items.plain_english: Even so, for the grace of those who do not know the truth, one should act in this way. And in the revered Picu scripture, O Lord, if sin is destroyed by remembrance alone, how can an expiation rite be required?

rows.grounds: states that the rite has been taught
states the freeing power of remembrance

items.question: What answer is given when the Goddess asks why expiation is declared?
premises: The Goddess prompts the question about the declared expiation rite.
The reply affirms that remembrance alone is truly sufficient.
Even a single utterance of remembrance can liberate one from action.
items.inference: At the highest level, remembrance itself has the power to free one, making formal expiation unnecessary in principle.
uncertainties: The specific form of remembrance or mantra uttered once is not named.
items.plain_english: When the Goddess asked why an expiation rite is declared, the answer was: it is true that remembrance alone, uttered even once, can liberate one here.

items.question: If remembrance frees the knower from all karma, why is the expiation rite still enjoined?
premises: One who knows remembrance, truth, and its parts is freed from the net of all action.
Social and scriptural order still needs protection.
The expiation rite is therefore enjoined as something to be done.
items.inference: Even when remembrance is sufficient in principle, the formal rite is retained to preserve order.
uncertainties: The phrase 'parts of remembrance and truth' may refer to specific doctrinal divisions not spelled out here.
items.plain_english: For one who knows remembrance, truth, and its parts, it can free one from the whole net of action. Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting order, the rite is still to be done and is enjoined.

the locus of doubt and confusion

items.question: Why do those fixed only in ritual conduct need formal expiation?
premises: Some practitioners do not know the truth and rely only on ritual conduct.
When their minds begin to waver, doubt undermines their practice.
This wavering leads to a loss of knowledge.
items.inference: For those grounded only in conduct, mental doubt is dangerous, so formal supports are needed to prevent the loss of knowledge.
items.plain_english: Those who do not know the truth and are fixed only in ritual conduct suffer a loss of knowledge when their minds begin to waver.

rows.grounds: the ideal inner stance of the practitioner
outward restraint to avoid disturbing others
the community that relies on external rules

items.question: How should a doubt-free practitioner behave among those dependent on scripture and conduct?
premises: A practitioner may inwardly be free from doubt.
Others may remain always dependent on scripture and ritual conduct.
Mixing practices can create confusion for such people.
items.inference: Even an inwardly free practitioner should act with restraint and avoid creating confusion in a rule-bound community.
uncertainties: The exact form of concealment or restraint is left unspecified.
items.plain_english: Therefore, if one is free from doubt, one should remain restrained and avoid creating confusion in practice among those who always depend on scripture and conduct.

rows.grounds: the expiation must actually be carried out
those dependent on scripture and conduct
the domain where doubt would arise

items.question: What should be done if confusion of practice has already occurred?
premises: Confusion of practice may arise despite restraint.
Such confusion can make others waver about the meaning of scripture.
Expiation can restore confidence and stability.
items.inference: If confusion occurs, one should seek and perform expiation so that others do not become doubtful about scriptural meaning.
items.plain_english: Or, if confusion of practice arises, one should seek and perform expiation so that their minds do not become unsteady about the meaning of scripture.

items.question: What expiation is prescribed in the Shiva-hand rite and what exception applies?
premises: The Shiva-hand rite formerly enjoined recitation of a weapon mantra.
Reciting it a hundred times brings freedom from fault.
The killing of a woman is explicitly excluded from this remedy.
items.inference: Mantric recitation can expiate many faults, but some transgressions are treated as beyond this ordinary remedy.
uncertainties: The exact identity of the weapon mantra is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: In the rite called Shiva-hand, it was formerly enjoined that by reciting this weapon mantra a hundred times one is freed, except in the case of killing a woman.

items.question: How grave is the fault of destroying a woman according to the Ratnamala?
premises: The Ratnamala addresses the case of transgressing a vow.
Destroying a woman is described as a great fault.
The consequence stated is everlasting hell.
items.inference: The text treats violence against a woman as an exceptionally severe transgression not covered by ordinary expiation.
uncertainties: The term 'śakti' is read here as 'woman' in line with the context, though it can have other senses elsewhere.
items.plain_english: In the revered Ratnamala, when a vow has been transgressed, it is said: from destroying a woman comes a great fault and everlasting hell, O beloved.

items.question: What expiation is declared for Kula members and how are vows purified?
premises: An expiation is declared for those born in the Kula in the case of the wicked knife.
An earlier revered text gives a method for purifying vows.
The next verses present that method.
items.inference: The tradition provides specific expiatory procedures for Kula transgressions and for restoring broken vows.
uncertainties: The expression 'wicked knife' is terse and may refer to a specific violent offense.
items.plain_english: For those born in the Kula, expiation for the wicked knife has been declared. And in the revered earlier text, what is enjoined for the purification of vows is as follows.

items.question: What recitation is prescribed when an unauthorized person sees consecrated things?
premises: Consecrated things may be seen by someone without authority.
Such a transgression requires purification.
Recitation of Malini or Matrika is prescribed as the remedy.
items.inference: Large-scale mantra recitation serves as expiation for violations involving unauthorized access to consecrated matters.
uncertainties: The exact range covered by 'and so forth' after consecrated things is not specified.
items.plain_english: If consecrated things and the like are seen by someone without authority, Malini or Matrika should be recited up to three hundred thousand times.

items.question: Which serious offenders are said in the Brahmayamala to require expiation?
premises: The Brahmayamala prescribes expiation for grave offenses.
The list includes killing a brahmin and violating the guru's bed.
It also includes stealing the substances used by the heroes.
items.inference: The text enumerates major transgressions that demand formal expiation according to the Brahmayamala.
uncertainties: The exact nature of 'hero substance' depends on ritual context not detailed here.
items.plain_english: In the revered Brahmayamala it is said that expiation must be performed by a killer of a brahmin, by one who approaches the guru's bed, and likewise by one who steals the hero's ritual substances.

items.question: What additional offenses requiring expiation are listed after the first group?
premises: The list of grave offenders continues.
It includes theft of divine property, striking sacred forms, and breaking a linga.
It also includes neglecting daily rites and falling from proper discipline.
items.inference: Expiation applies both to direct sacrilege and to serious neglect of obligatory religious discipline.
uncertainties: The phrase 'own measure and equipment' is compact and may refer to prescribed personal or ritual standards.
items.plain_english: Also included are one who takes the property of the gods or strikes a sacred form, one who breaks a linga, and one who neglects the daily rites and has fallen from his proper measure and equipment.

items.question: How should expiation be scaled for violent and disruptive offenses?
premises: The list includes maiming a woman, killing a yogi or knower, and disrupting occasional rites.
These offenses require mantra recitation as expiation.
The recitation increases in a doubling sequence starting from a hundred thousand.
items.inference: More severe or disruptive transgressions call for progressively greater amounts of mantra recitation.
uncertainties: The exact mapping of each offense to each doubling step is not fully specified.
items.plain_english: One who maims a woman, kills a yogi or a knower, or disrupts the occasional rites should recite mantras in a doubling sequence beginning with a hundred thousand.

items.question: What discipline accompanies expiation when one goes astray through desire with a messenger woman?
premises: A specific offense involves going to a messenger woman elsewhere while deluded by desire.
Expiation in this case is not recitation alone.
It must be joined with a vow, limited eating, and celibacy.
items.inference: Certain transgressions require both mantra recitation and a regimen of bodily and moral restraint.
uncertainties: The ritual role of the 'messenger woman' is context-dependent and not fully explained here.
items.plain_english: If, deluded by desire, one has gone to take a messenger woman elsewhere, one should undertake the expiation joined with some vow, eating little and observing celibacy.

items.question: What expiation is prescribed for that desire-driven offense and what closes major rites?
premises: The Brahmayamala prescribes a hundred-thousandfold recitation for the stated offense.
Major rites such as initiation, consecration, and occasional rites require a proper conclusion.
Worship of the guru is enjoined at their end.
items.inference: The section moves from expiation to closure, showing that major ritual occasions culminate in guru worship.
items.plain_english: Then one should perform a recitation of a hundred thousand, as it is said in the Brahmayamala. At the end of initiation, consecration, and occasional rites, worship of the guru is required.

items.question: When should guru worship be done and what kind of guru is to be honored?
premises: Guru worship is to be done on the next day and always, according to the Siddhayogishvari teaching.
The guru must possess the previously stated marks.
The guru must be a seer who knows the true principle of the Trika.
items.inference: The concluding worship is directed to a properly qualified guru grounded in Trika realization.
uncertainties: The 'previously stated marks' refer back to qualifications not listed in this verse.
items.plain_english: According to the teaching of the Siddhayogishvari, it should always be done on the next day. The guru to be honored is one endowed with the previously stated marks, a seer who knows the true principle of the Trika.

items.question: Which guru should be accepted for worship and how is the ritual seat prepared?
premises: Only the properly qualified guru should always be accepted.
Another person present in the circle should not replace him.
A svastika and a suitable seat are prepared for the worship.
items.inference: Guru worship requires both correct recognition of the qualified teacher and proper ritual preparation of the seat.
items.plain_english: That guru should always be accepted, leaving aside any other, even if another is present in the circle. Having made a svastika there, one should prepare a golden or similar seat.

items.question: What is worshiped first and how is the guru invited to preside?

items.inference: Guru worship begins by honoring the full path in that locus and then formally requesting the guru's presence.

items.plain_english: Having prepared it, one should worship the path present there in its full extent. Then, with devotion, one should request the guru to preside there.

items.question: How is the guru to be worshiped once he is present in the ritual place?

items.plain_english: There he should be worshiped with his own mantras, in order, with offerings of flowers, incense, and arghya, and with touching, fine garments, food offerings, and libations.

items.question: What should the disciple offer to the guru after completing the worship?

After worship, the disciple honors the guru with gifts.

items.inference: Guru worship culminates in generous giving and inward self-offering by the disciple.
items.plain_english: Having worshiped him in all directions, the disciple should honor him with gifts. With devout awareness, one should give him all that one has and even oneself.

items.question: Why must even a knower of truth satisfy the guru with gifts?
premises: The disciple satisfies the guru completely with gifts.
Even one who knows the truth is bound by the debt incurred toward the guru.
Fulfilling that obligation establishes proper fitness for authority.
items.inference: Guru worship and gifts are not merely symbolic; they discharge a real obligation that grounds the disciple's authority.
items.plain_english: But having completely satisfied the guru with gifts, even one who knows the truth, because of the bond of debt to him, attains fitness for authority.

items.question: What consequence follows from neglecting guru worship according to the Skandayamala?
premises: Guru worship is a required observance.
Neglecting it delays spiritual qualification.
The Skandayamala states that one is born for a hundred births before gaining authority and then liberation.
items.inference: Failure to perform guru worship is presented as a serious obstacle that postpones both authority and liberation.
uncertainties: The 'hundred births' may be rhetorical for a very long time rather than a literal count.
items.plain_english: According to the Skandayamala, one who does not perform guru worship is born for a hundred births; then, becoming fit for authority, one attains liberation.
